questions.q: What does trunk-based development require beyond just "merging to main often"?
options: That main always stay in a deployable state, backed by strong automated test coverage
That every developer work entirely without branches, including for PR review
That releases happen exactly once per year
That feature flags never be used
questions.explain: Trunk-based development's strict requirement is that main stays deployable at all times, which demands real automated test coverage since there's no long-lived branch buffering unfinished work from main.

questions.q: Why does a feature branch that stays open for several weeks become a high-risk merge?
options: Because Git deletes branches older than two weeks automatically
Because the longer it diverges from main, the more main changes underneath it unreconciled, concentrating risk into one large, difficult merge
Because long-lived branches cannot be pushed to a remote
Because GitHub charges extra for long-lived branches
questions.explain: Deferring integration lets main and the branch drift apart for weeks with nothing reconciling the divergence, turning the eventual merge into a concentrated, high-risk event rather than a series of small, manageable ones.

questions.q: What is a feature flag (feature toggle)?
options: A Git branch naming convention
A runtime switch that lets merged, in-progress functionality stay inactive in production until it's ready
A required field on every pull request
A type of merge conflict marker
questions.explain: A feature flag decouples merging code from releasing it to users — the code can be merged into main continuously while staying inactive (flagged off) until the feature is actually ready.

questions.q: In a Salesforce context, what might implement a feature flag, per this lesson?
options: A Custom Metadata Type record, Custom Setting, or custom permission checked at runtime
A new sandbox created for every feature
A Git tag applied to the production branch
The Setup Audit Trail
questions.explain: The lesson gives Custom Metadata Type records, Custom Settings, or custom permissions as realistic Salesforce mechanisms for a runtime flag controlling whether a feature's logic executes.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is trunk-based development incompatible with a scheduled Salesforce release train?
options: Yes, release trains require long-lived feature branches by definition

No — many teams merge small, short-lived branches into a shared integration branch continuously, and the release train is about when a stable point gets promoted through environments, not about long developer isolation
Yes, trunk-based development forbids any use of QA or UAT sandboxes
No, because trunk-based development has nothing to do with branches at all
questions.explain: The lesson frames the choice as orthogonal: how long individual developer branches live before merging is separate from how releases get scheduled and promoted through environments — the two can coexist.
